title: Guru Hargobind's gurpurab
hook: remembered with the two swords of miri and piri

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Amar Das's gurpurab, and your line: eighty-four steps. Did you take one rushed task slowly, step by step? We skip ahead today, past the fifth Guru, to his son. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

Picture a boy of about eleven, whose father has just been killed. Not in an accident. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, the man who built the Harmandir Sahib and gathered the Granth, has died in custody in Lahore, in 1606. The Sikhs are grieving and afraid. And on the day the boy becomes the sixth Guru, he does something no Guru before him had done. He asks for two swords, and he puts on both. Today: Guru Hargobind's gurpurab.
screen: `A BOY OF ABOUT ELEVEN.` → `HIS FATHER KILLED IN 1606.` → `HE PUTS ON TWO SWORDS.`

segments.voice: Guru Hargobind was born in 1595, near Amritsar. You've met his birth already: the shabad of Guru Arjan's joy when his son arrived. After his father's execution, he became Guru, and the two swords he wore became one of the most important ideas in Sikh life. One sword was miri: worldly power, responsibility in the world, the duty to protect. The other was piri: spiritual authority, the life of devotion and the Name. Miri and piri. The words come from Persian: mir, a ruler, and pir, a spiritual guide. The point wasn't two separate lives. It was that a Sikh holds both at once. Devotion without courage can abandon the weak. Power without devotion turns cruel. The two swords keep each other honest. He gave the idea a building. Facing the Harmandir Sahib, he raised a platform called the Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One. The Harmandir is where the Word is sung. The Akal Takht is where the community gathers to decide, and act. Even today, they stand looking at each other across the same courtyard. Guru Hargobind kept horses and armed followers, and fought battles with Mughal forces. He was also, tradition remembers, a man of deep devotion who kept the kirtan going morning and evening. Sikhs see the Khanda emblem, with its swords on either side, as carrying the same idea. His gurpurab is marked with kirtan, and in many places with displays of gatka, the Sikh martial art. Two swords, one Guru.
screen: `AFTER HIS FATHER'S EXECUTION.` · `MIRI AND PIRI: TWO SWORDS.` · `EACH KEEPS THE OTHER HONEST.` · `THE AKAL TAKHT FACES THE HARMANDIR.` · then, large: `TWO SWORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand tall. If you can, stand up. Feet planted, shoulders back, chin level. Feel your weight evenly on both feet: one side for your duties in the world, one for your inner life. Notice if you lean more on one. Gently even them out. Breathe in strength, breathe out stillness. If you can't stand, sit as tall as you can. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, standing like that. The bell holds the time.
Guru Hargobind's gurpurab. The sixth Guru's birthday, remembered with the two swords of miri and piri, worldly duty and spiritual life, held together.
Your line: two swords. Today, notice one place where you need more courage, and one where you need more devotion, and give a little to each. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: On Guru Hargobind's gurpurab, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and some communities display gatka; Sikhs remember his two swords of miri and piri and the Akal Takht he founded.

original.note: Punjabi: worldly and spiritual authority, from Persian mir, ruler, and pir, guide.

trapdoor: what you thought: the swords made the Sikhs a military group.
what it means: they hold duty in the world and devotion to God together.
what a scholar hears: miri and piri draw on Persian mir and pir; the Akal Takht (founded 1606) faces the Harmandir as a seat of temporal authority.
